lines: Let's zoom out. What's the authors' read on why all this happens?

A few ideas I found genuinely useful. First, cognitive forcing. The individual benefit may come less from the agent having a spec, and more from the developer articulating goals before delegating. If that's true, any practice that forces planning first, including the plan modes in Claude Code and Cursor, should deliver much of the same value.
And that's testable. They propose the experiment: a spec written and given to the agent, a spec written and withheld, and no spec at all, on the same tasks.

Second, the work and the benefit land on different people. The author pays to write the spec. Teammates and future agents collect the benefit later. That's an old pattern from groupware research, and it explains why individuals persist with SDD while their teams resist.
Third is the irony of automation.

Humans stay responsible for monitoring work they're less and less involved in. When one agent writes the spec, the code, and the tests, one misunderstanding propagates through all three. And delegating spec review to an agent removes the one point where a person decides what the system should do.

There's also a design-history wrinkle. OpenSpec keeps archived changes in the working tree. That makes history accessible to people, but agents read the working tree too, so they can run into outdated intent.
And most archived records are agent-written descriptions of what changed. Not why it changed. So keeping the history doesn't keep the reasoning.
